A hand-me-down is something — most often a piece of clothing, but also any object — that one person used to own or use, and then passed on to someone else to use after them, instead of throwing it away or selling it.

The key ideas baked into this word are:

  • The item is not new. It has already been owned and used.
  • It is given, not sold — passed along freely.
  • There is usually a chain of passing: from one person → to another person.

The most typical and classic situation for a hand-me-down is within a family with siblings, especially from an older child to a younger one.

Imagine a family with three children. The oldest child, aged 14, has a jacket. After a year or two, they grow out of it. Instead of buying a new jacket for the 11-year-old sibling, the parents simply give the older child's jacket to the middle child. Then, when the middle child grows out of it, it gets passed down again to the youngest child.

That jacket is a hand-me-down for the middle child, and a hand-me-down again for the youngest child.

This is the heart of the word.

Anything, really — but some things are far more commonly described this way than others.

Very commonly:

  • Clothes (shoes, jackets, school uniforms, jeans)
  • Toys and games
  • Bicycles
  • School bags and stationery
  • Books

Less commonly but still possible:

  • Furniture
  • Electronics (an old phone passed from a parent to a teenager)
  • A car passed from a parent to a child
  • Kitchen items

If it has been used by one person and then given to another person to use, it qualifies as a hand-me-down.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is important to understand, because words carry emotional weight beyond their dictionary meaning.

The word "hand-me-down" carries a slightly humble or modest tone. It quietly tells you that the item is not brand new, not chosen fresh from a store — it is pre-owned. Depending on the context, this feeling can go in different directions:

Sometimes neutral or even warm: In many families, passing things down is completely normal, practical, and even a loving gesture. There is no shame in it — it is simply how things work.

Sometimes slightly negative: If someone feels embarrassed about never having new things of their own — always wearing what their older sibling wore first — the word can carry a sense of lacking or being second in line. A child might say with some frustration, "I'm tired of wearing hand-me-downs. I want something that's actually mine."

The word never means something stolen, sold, or borrowed. It is specifically about something given freely, passed along within a family or social circle.

• One item → a hand-me-down (singular)
  • Multiple items → hand-me-downs (plural)

The plural is actually very common, perhaps even more common than the singular, because hand-me-downs often come in batches — a whole bag of clothes, not just one shirt.

"My cousins sent over a box of hand-me-downs for my son."
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are clear, natural examples showing the word in action:

  • "This sweater is a hand-me-down from my older brother."
  • "Growing up, almost everything I wore was a hand-me-down."
  • "She didn't mind hand-me-downs — she actually liked getting her sister's old clothes."
  • "The bicycle was a hand-me-down from a neighbor's kid."
  • "My dad gave me his old laptop as a hand-me-down when he bought a new one."
An Important Distinction: Not Just Any Used Item

A hand-me-down is not the same as a second-hand item bought from a shop or a stranger. The word specifically implies a personal connection — it moves between people who know each other, usually family members or close friends. It is passed down as a gesture, not as a transaction.

If you buy an old coat from a thrift store, that coat is "second-hand" or "used" — but it is not, strictly speaking, your hand-me-down. However, if your aunt gave you her old coat because she no longer needed it, that coat is a hand-me-down.

In more advanced or expressive writing, "hand-me-down" can be used figuratively — meaning it can describe non-physical things that are passed along from one person to another without much original thought.

For example:

  • "He held onto hand-me-down beliefs from his parents without ever questioning them."
  • "The culture was full of hand-me-down traditions that no one truly understood anymore."

Here, the word paints a picture of something inherited uncritically — ideas, beliefs, habits, or traditions that were just accepted from whoever came before, like wearing a shirt without choosing it yourself.
A hand-me-down is a used item — especially clothing — passed freely from one person to another (often from older to younger) because the original owner no longer needs it.
